stem: How many particles are there in one mole of a substance?
explanation: One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, 6.02 × 10²³. The value 12 comes from carbon-12, which defines the scale but is not the number of particles.

stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure?
explanation: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at r.t.p. Note the unit: 24 cm³ is a thousand times too small.

stem: Which statement defines the relative atomic mass of an element?

options.text: The average mass of its atoms compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
The number of protons in one atom of the element
The total number of protons and neutrons in one atom
The mass in grams of one atom of the element

explanation: Ar is an average mass relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom. Protons + neutrons is the mass number of a single atom, not Ar.

stem: The relative atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5. Why is it not a whole number?

options.text: Chlorine atoms can gain an electron
Chlorine is a mixture of isotopes with different masses

explanation: Ar is an average over the isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, weighted by how common each is, which gives 35.5.

stem: What is the relative molecular mass (Mr) of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄? (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
What is the Mr of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
explanation: 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100. The answer 68 comes from forgetting to multiply oxygen by 3.

stem: What is the Mr of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂? (H = 1, O = 16, Ca = 40)
explanation: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74. Everything inside the bracket is multiplied by 2; 57 comes from ignoring the bracket.

stem: How many moles are in 8.0 g of methane, CH₄? (H = 1, C = 12)
explanation: Mr of CH₄ = 12 + 4 = 16, so moles = 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.5 mol.

stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? (H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)
What volume does 0.5 mol of carbon dioxide occupy at r.t.p.?
explanation: Volume = moles × 24 = 0.5 × 24 = 12 dm³. The identity of the gas does not matter.

stem: How many moles of gas are in 600 cm³ at r.t.p.?
explanation: The volume is in cm³, so divide by 24 000: 600 ÷ 24 000 = 0.025 mol. Dividing by 24 gives the wrong answer of 25.

stem: How many water molecules are in 2 mol of water?
explanation: Number of molecules = 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²⁴.

stem: Which sample contains the same number of molecules as 2 g of hydrogen, H₂? (H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
explanation: 2 g of H₂ is 1 mol. 32 g of O₂ is also 1 mol (Mr = 32), so it contains the same number of molecules. 16 g of O₂ and 14 g of N₂ are each 0.5 mol.

stem: One mole of which substance contains the greatest number of atoms?
explanation: Each CH₄ molecule has 5 atoms; NH₃ has 4; CO₂ and H₂O have 3. The same number of molecules means CH₄ has the most atoms.

stem: What is the mass of 48 dm³ of oxygen gas, O₂, at r.t.p.? (O = 16)
explanation: Moles = 48 ÷ 24 = 2 mol. Mass = 2 × 32 = 64 g.

stem: At r.t.p., 1 mol of hydrogen and 1 mol of carbon dioxide are compared. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They have different masses but the same volume
They have the same mass and the same volume
They have different masses and different volumes
They have the same mass but different volumes

explanation: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p., but their molar masses differ (H₂ = 2 g, CO₂ = 44 g).

stem: How many moles of atoms are in 4.6 g of sodium? (Na = 23)
explanation: Moles = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.2 mol.

stem: What is the Mr of aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃? (O = 16, Al = 27, S = 32)
A sample of a gas has a mass of 11 g and a volume of 6 dm³ at r.t.p. Which gas could it be? (C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
explanation: Moles = 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol. Molar mass = 11 ÷ 0.25 = 44 g/mol, which matches CO₂ (12 + 32 = 44).

stem: Which of the following has a mass of 16 g? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
explanation: 0.5 mol × 32 g/mol = 16 g. 1 mol of O₂ = 32 g; 0.5 mol of O atoms = 8 g; 2 mol of CH₄ = 32 g.

stem: Magnesium nitrate has the formula Mg(NO₃)₂. (N = 14, O = 16, Mg = 24)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define one mole of a substance.
parts.markScheme: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules or ions) [1]. Accept 'Avogadro's number of particles'.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of magnesium nitrate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles in 37 g of magnesium nitrate.
parts.markScheme: moles = 37 ÷ 148 [1] = 0.25 mol [1]. Allow error carried forward from (b).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of nitrate ions in this 37 g sample.

stem: A gas syringe collects 360 cm³ of ammonia gas, NH₃, at room temperature and pressure. (H = 1, N = 14; one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p.)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of ammonia collected.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of ammonia collected.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A second syringe contains 360 cm³ of hydrogen at r.t.p. Compare the number of molecules in the two syringes.
parts.markScheme: Same number of molecules, because equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of moles (molecules) [1].

stem: Chlorine has two isotopes: chlorine-35 (75% of atoms) and chlorine-37 (25% of atoms).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the relative atomic mass of chlorine is not a whole number.
parts.markScheme: Ar is the (weighted) average mass of the isotopes present [1].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine. Show your working.

stem: Which of these quantities is a vector?
explanation: Displacement has both size and direction. Speed, distance and time have size only.

stem: Acceleration is defined as

options.text: the rate of change of distance
the rate of change of velocity

explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken. 'Speed in a given direction' is the definition of velocity.

stem: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
explanation: Acceleration is velocity (m/s) per second, which gives m/s².

stem: A car travels 150 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?
explanation: Average speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 6 = 25 m/s.

stem: A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
On a distance–time graph, a horizontal straight line shows that the object is
explanation: Distance is not changing, so the object is not moving. The gradient (speed) is zero.

stem: What does the gradient of a distance–time graph represent?
explanation: Gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time = speed.

stem: A speed–time graph is a straight line starting at the origin and sloping upwards. What does this show?
explanation: A straight line means constant gradient, so acceleration is constant (uniform). Starting at the origin means the object starts from rest.

stem: An object accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 6 s. How far does it travel in this time?
explanation: Distance = area under the speed–time graph = ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m.

stem: What is the approximate acceleration of free fall near the Earth's surface?
explanation: g is about 9.8 m/s², usually taken as 10 m/s² in calculations.

stem: A stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed after 3 s? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: v = u + gt = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m/s. 45 m is the distance fallen, not the speed.

stem: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a uniform deceleration of 4 m/s². How long does it take to stop?
explanation: v = u + at gives 0 = 20 − 4t, so t = 5 s.

stem: A falling object reaches terminal velocity when

options.text: air resistance is greater than its weight

explanation: When the forces balance, the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and the velocity is constant.

stem: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity and then opens her parachute. What happens next?

options.text: She speeds up, then falls at a higher terminal velocity
She stops moving for a moment, then falls again
She keeps falling at the same velocity
She slows down, then falls at a lower terminal velocity

explanation: Opening the parachute increases air resistance above her weight, so she decelerates. As she slows, air resistance falls until it equals her weight again, giving a lower terminal velocity.

stem: A hammer and a feather are dropped together from the same height in a vacuum. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The hammer lands first because it is heavier
The feather lands first because it is lighter
They land at the same time
The feather floats and does not fall

explanation: With no air resistance, both fall with the same acceleration g, whatever their mass.

stem: A car drives round a roundabout at a constant speed of 30 km/h. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its velocity is constant because its speed is constant
Its velocity is changing because its direction is changing

explanation: Velocity includes direction. A change of direction means the velocity changes, so the motion is non-uniform.

stem: An athlete runs one complete lap of a 400 m track in 50 s and finishes at the starting point. What is her average velocity?
explanation: Her displacement is zero because she finishes where she started, so her average velocity is 0. Her average speed is 400 ÷ 50 = 8 m/s.

stem: A trolley moves at a constant 10 m/s for 4 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 2 s. What is the total distance travelled?
explanation: Constant-speed part: 10 × 4 = 40 m. Deceleration part: ½ × 2 × 10 = 10 m. Total = 50 m.

stem: A steel ball bearing is dropped into a tall tube of thick oil. Which describes its motion after the first moment?

options.text: It keeps accelerating at 10 m/s² until it hits the bottom
It falls at a steady (terminal) velocity
It slows down and stops halfway
It speeds up and slows down repeatedly

explanation: The drag from oil is large, so the ball bearing reaches terminal velocity very quickly and then falls at constant speed.

stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 s. How far does it travel?
explanation: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 5² = 25 m.

stem:
The table shows the speed of a minibus taxi during a short journey.

| Time / s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Speed / m/s | 0 | 4 | 8 | 8 | 8 | 0 |

The taxi accelerates uniformly for the first 4 s, travels at constant speed from 4 s to 8 s, and decelerates uniformly from 8 s to 10 s.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of the taxi during the first 4 s.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance travelled in the 10 s.
parts.markScheme: 0–4 s: ½ × 4 × 8 = 16 m; 4–8 s: 4 × 8 = 32 m; 8–10 s: ½ × 2 × 8 = 8 m [2 for the areas, 1 for any two correct]; total = 56 m [1].

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
parts.markScheme: average speed = 56 ÷ 10 [1] = 5.6 m/s [1]. Allow ecf from (b).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe the motion of the taxi between 8 s and 10 s.
parts.markScheme: Uniform deceleration from 8 m/s to rest (at 4 m/s²) [1].

stem: A learner drops a stone from rest off a cliff. It takes 4.0 s to reach the water below. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance unless told otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the stone just before it hits the water.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the height of the cliff.
parts.markScheme: s = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 4² [1] = 80 m [1]. Accept area under the speed–time graph = ½ × 4 × 40.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In reality, the stone hits the water at a lower speed. Explain why.
parts.markScheme: Air resistance acts upwards, opposing the motion, so the resultant force (and therefore the acceleration) is less than for free fall [1].

stem: A skydiver jumps from an aeroplane, falls for some time, and then opens her parachute.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define terminal velocity.
parts.markScheme: The constant (maximum) velocity reached when the air resistance on a falling object equals its weight [1].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe and explain how her velocity changes from the moment she jumps until she lands. Refer to the forces acting on her.
parts.markScheme: Any four of: at first weight > air resistance, so she accelerates [1]; air resistance increases as speed increases, so acceleration decreases [1]; air resistance = weight, so resultant force is zero and she reaches terminal velocity [1]; when the parachute opens, air resistance > weight, so she decelerates [1]; she reaches a new, lower terminal velocity when the forces balance again [1].

stem: Which statement defines diffusion?

options.text: Movement of water through a partially permeable membrane
Movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy
Net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
Movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration

explanation: Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient, from higher to lower concentration, by random movement.

stem: Osmosis is the movement of

options.text: solute molecules from a concentrated to a dilute solution
water molecules from a concentrated to a dilute solution
any molecules through a fully permeable membrane
water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution

explanation: In osmosis, water moves from higher water concentration (dilute solution) to lower water concentration (concentrated solution) through a partially permeable membrane.

stem: Which process needs energy from respiration?
explanation: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, which needs energy from respiration.

stem: Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?

options.text: Making the concentration gradient less steep
Increasing the distance particles must travel

explanation: At a higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion is faster.

stem: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
explanation: Water enters by osmosis and the vacuole swells, pressing the cell against the wall. The wall stops it bursting.

stem: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
explanation: Water enters by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall to resist the swelling, so the cell bursts.

stem: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. What would you see under the microscope?

options.text: The cell swells and the wall breaks
The cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall

explanation: Water leaves by osmosis, so the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall. This is plasmolysis.

stem: The concentration of nitrate ions is higher inside root hair cells than in the soil water. How do the root hairs take in more nitrate ions?
explanation: Moving ions from lower concentration (soil) to higher concentration (cell) is against the gradient, so it needs active transport.

stem: Why does a plant wilt on a hot, dry day?

options.text: Its cells gain too much water and burst
Its cells lose water, become flaccid and lose turgor
It takes in too many mineral ions

explanation: When water is lost faster than it is taken up, cells become flaccid and can no longer support the leaves and stem.

stem: Potato strips were placed in sucrose solutions. % change in mass: 0.0 mol/dm³: +12%; 0.2 mol/dm³: +5%; 0.4 mol/dm³: −2%; 0.6 mol/dm³: −8%. What is the concentration of the potato cell sap closest to?
explanation: There is no change in mass where the solution matches the cell sap. The change goes from +5% to −2% between 0.2 and 0.4 mol/dm³.

stem: A partially permeable membrane

options.text: lets small molecules such as water pass but not larger ones such as sucrose
lets only large molecules pass through

explanation: Partially permeable membranes let small molecules like water through but not larger solute molecules.

stem: Why does oxygen move from the air in the alveoli into the blood?

options.text: The blood actively pumps oxygen in
The oxygen concentration is higher in the blood than in the alveoli
The oxygen concentration is higher in the alveoli than in the blood
Water carries oxygen across by osmosis

explanation: Oxygen diffuses down its concentration gradient, from the alveoli (higher) into the blood (lower).

stem: Cotton wool soaked in ammonia is placed at one end of a glass tube and cotton wool soaked in hydrochloric acid at the other. A white ring forms nearer the acid end. What does this show?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid particles diffuse faster than ammonia particles
Ammonia particles are smaller and diffuse faster
Both gases diffuse at the same rate

explanation: The ammonia travelled further in the same time, so it diffused faster. This is because ammonia molecules are lighter than hydrogen chloride molecules.

stem: Passive transport is the movement of substances

options.text: against a concentration gradient using energy
down a concentration gradient without using energy from respiration

explanation: Passive processes such as diffusion and osmosis move substances down a gradient without using energy from respiration.

stem: A Visking tubing bag containing sugar solution is placed in a beaker of pure water. After an hour the bag has swollen. Why?

options.text: Sugar left the bag by diffusion
Water left the bag by active transport
Sugar entered the bag from the water
Water entered the bag by osmosis

explanation: The water outside is more dilute, so water moves into the bag through the partially permeable tubing by osmosis.

stem: How is active transport different from diffusion?

options.text: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy
Active transport is faster at lower temperatures
Active transport does not need a membrane

explanation: Active transport uses energy from respiration to move substances from low to high concentration. Diffusion is passive and moves substances down the gradient.

stem: Root hair cells are treated with a poison that stops respiration. Which process would stop first?

options.text: Diffusion of oxygen into the cells
Uptake of mineral ions by active transport
Diffusion of carbon dioxide out of the cells

explanation: Active transport needs energy from respiration. Osmosis and diffusion are passive, so they can continue.

stem: What happens to the rate of diffusion when the concentration gradient becomes steeper?
explanation: A bigger difference in concentration means a faster net movement of particles.

stem: Osmosis is a special type of
explanation: Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane.

stem: Which describes a flaccid plant cell?

options.text: Cell is full of water and pressing firmly against the wall
Cell has gained mineral ions by active transport
Cell has lost some water; vacuole smaller and cell soft, but membrane still touching the wall

explanation: A flaccid cell has lost water and turgor but is not yet plasmolysed, so the membrane still touches the wall.

stem:
A learner placed potato strips of equal size in sucrose solutions for 30 minutes and recorded the results.

| Sucrose concentration / mol/dm³ | 0.0 | 0.2 | 0.4 | 0.6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial mass / g | 2.50 | 2.50 | 2.50 | 2.50 |
| Final mass / g | 2.80 | 2.62 | 2.45 | 2.30 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in mass of the strip in 0.6 mol/dm³ sucrose.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the strip in 0.0 mol/dm³ gained mass.
parts.markScheme: The water/solution was more dilute than the cell sap (higher water concentration outside) [1]; water entered the cells by osmosis through the partially permeable membrane [1].

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Estimate the concentration of the potato cell sap. Give a reason.
parts.markScheme: About 0.35 mol/dm³ (accept any value between 0.3 and 0.4) [1]; this is where there would be no change in mass, so no net movement of water [1].

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: State one variable that should be kept constant.
parts.markScheme: Any one of: size/surface area of strips, time in solution, temperature, type/source of potato, method of blotting [1].

stem: Root hair cells absorb both water and mineral ions from the soil.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how water enters a root hair cell.
parts.markScheme: By osmosis [1]; from the soil water (higher water concentration / more dilute) into the cell sap (lower water concentration / more concentrated) through the partially permeable membrane [1].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why root hair cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.markScheme: Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport, against their concentration gradient [1]; this needs energy, which mitochondria release by respiration [1].

stem: A plant cell and a red blood cell are each placed in pure water.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe what happens to each cell.
parts.markScheme: Plant cell becomes turgid / swells but does not burst [1]; red blood cell swells and bursts [1].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the difference in your answers to (a).
parts.markScheme: Water enters both cells by osmosis [1]; the plant cell wall is strong and resists further expansion, but the red blood cell has no cell wall [1].

stem: Which statement best describes development?

options.text: An increase in the number of factories
A process of positive change that improves people's quality of life
An increase in a country's population
A rise in the price of exports

explanation: Development is broader than economic growth. It includes social, political and environmental improvements in people's lives.

stem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the total value of goods and services produced

options.text: within a country's borders in a year
by a country's citizens anywhere in the world in a year
by the government only in a year
for export only in a year

explanation: GDP counts production inside the country's borders. GNP/GNI counts production by a country's citizens and companies wherever they are.

stem: What is the main difference between GNP and GDP?

options.text: GNP includes net income earned from abroad
GNP is always smaller than GDP

explanation: GNP = GDP + net income from abroad. It can be bigger or smaller than GDP.

stem: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Index (HDI)?
explanation: The UNDP publishes the HDI in its Human Development Report.

stem: The Human Development Index combines measures of

options.text: life expectancy, education and income per person

explanation: The HDI combines a long and healthy life, knowledge (education) and a decent standard of living (income per person).

stem: Why can GDP per capita give a misleading picture of development?

options.text: It is an average that hides how unequally income is shared
It counts the informal sector twice

explanation: A few very wealthy people can raise the average while most people remain poor. GDP per capita also ignores the informal sector and social conditions.

stem: Why are political aspects of development difficult to measure?

options.text: They are the same in every country
They can be counted exactly from election results
They are mostly qualitative and partly subjective

explanation: Freedom, democracy and human rights are hard to put into numbers, and governments may hide information.

stem: During the Cold War, the term 'Second World' referred to

options.text: the communist bloc led by the USSR

explanation: First World = Western capitalist; Second World = communist bloc; Third World = developing countries.

stem: Which group of countries are known as Newly Industrialised Countries (NICs)?
explanation: The 'Asian Tigers' (South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, Hong Kong) are the classic NICs. They industrialised rapidly from the 1960s.

stem: Australia is in the southern hemisphere but is classified as part of the 'North'. Why?

options.text: Australia was a colony of Brazil
The term 'North' only refers to Europe
The Brandt Line is based on level of development, not geography

explanation: The North–South divide (Brandt Line) separates richer and poorer countries, so it bends around Australia and New Zealand.

stem: Which is a typical characteristic of a developing country?

options.text: Most workers in the tertiary sector
High birth rate and a large share of workers in farming

explanation: Developing countries usually have high birth rates and many people in primary-sector work such as farming.

stem: Which theory argues that poor countries are underdeveloped because rich 'core' countries exploit them?
explanation: Dependency theory sees the periphery as supplying cheap raw materials and labour to benefit the core.

stem: Rostow's 'stages of economic growth' is an example of
explanation: Rostow's five-stage model, from traditional society to high mass consumption, is the best-known modernisation theory.

stem: Sustainable development is development that

options.text: meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
stops all use of natural resources

explanation: This is the Brundtland Report (1987) definition.

stem: Which reason helps explain why a landlocked country may develop more slowly?

options.text: Transport costs for imports and exports are higher

explanation: Without a coastline, goods must pass through neighbouring countries' ports. This adds cost and dependence.

stem: Development can be measured using economic indicators.

parts.prompt: Explain the difference between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross National Product (GNP).
parts.markScheme: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced within a country's borders [1] in a year [1]. GNP is GDP plus net income from abroad [1], i.e. the output of a country's citizens and companies wherever they are located [1].

stem: Some aspects of development are easier to measure than others.

parts.prompt: Give two reasons why the political aspects of development are difficult to measure.
parts.markScheme: Two reasons, each identified [1] and explained [1], e.g.: they are qualitative / hard to put into numbers [1], e.g. freedom of speech cannot be counted [1]; judgements are subjective [1], since people disagree on what counts as democracy [1]; governments may hide or distort information [1], so data is unreliable [1]; elections taking place does not show they were free and fair [1].

stem: Theories of development offer different explanations of poverty.

parts.prompt: Outline two differences between modernisation theory and dependency theory.
parts.markScheme: Two differences, 2 marks each: modernisation sees poverty caused by internal factors / traditional ways [1], while dependency blames external exploitation by rich core countries [1]; modernisation recommends following the Western path through industrialisation and investment [1], while dependency recommends reducing ties with the core, e.g. import substitution or regional co-operation [1]; modernisation sees trade/contact with rich countries as helpful [1], while dependency sees it as harmful [1].

stem:
The table shows development data for four countries, W, X, Y and Z. (The figures are invented for practice.)

| Country | GNI per capita (US$) | Life expectancy (years) | Adult literacy (%) | Infant mortality (per 1000 live births) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | 42 000 | 81 | 99 | 4 |
| X | 7 000 | 69 | 88 | 30 |
| Y | 900 | 58 | 55 | 70 |
| Z | 14 000 | 63 | 85 | 45 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Which country is the most developed? Use two pieces of evidence from the table.
parts.markScheme: Country W [1]; any two pieces of evidence with data, e.g. highest GNI per capita (US$42 000) [1], highest life expectancy (81) [1], lowest infant mortality (4 per 1000) [1], highest literacy (99%) [1]. Max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Country Z has a higher GNI per capita than country X but a lower life expectancy. Suggest two reasons why GNI per capita alone may not show the true level of development in Z.
parts.markScheme: Two reasons, each with explanation, e.g.: income may be unequally distributed, so most people are poor [1] and cannot afford health care [1]; wealth may come from one resource (e.g. mining) that employs few people [1] and is not spent on social services [1]; high disease burden (e.g. HIV/AIDS) [1] lowers life expectancy despite income [1]; government spending priorities may not favour health/education [1] [1]. Max 4.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest one other indicator not in the table that could be used to compare these countries. Explain why it is useful.
parts.markScheme: Valid indicator [1], e.g. access to clean water, doctors per 1000 people, HDI, energy use per person, % in primary sector; explanation of what it shows about quality of life or development [2].

stem: According to Matthew 22:37–39, what are the two greatest commandments?

options.text: Do not steal and do not kill
Keep the Sabbath and honour your parents
Love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself

explanation: Jesus summarised the Law as love of God and love of neighbour.

stem: Which Bible passage describes love as patient, kind and not boastful?
explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 lists the qualities of love.

stem: The Greek word for unconditional, self-giving love is
explanation: Agape is the selfless love Christians believe God shows and expects them to show everyone.

stem: In the Parable of the Good Samaritan, who turns out to be the true 'neighbour'?

options.text: The Samaritan who helped the injured man

explanation: The Samaritan, an outsider to the Jews, showed mercy. Jesus taught that your neighbour is anyone in need.

stem: Which teaching of Jesus is found in Matthew 5:43–44?

options.text: Love only those who love you
Give to Caesar what is Caesar's
Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you

explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus extended love even to enemies.

stem: Which action of Jesus best shows humble, serving love?

options.text: Turning over tables in the temple

explanation: Washing feet was a servant's job. By doing it, Jesus showed humble service (John 13).

stem: On the cross Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' What does this show?
explanation: Forgiving those who were killing him shows love that does not seek revenge (Luke 23:34).

stem: Jesus touched and healed a man with leprosy (Mark 1:40–42). Why is this a powerful example of love?

options.text: Lepers were outcasts whom people avoided touching
The man was one of his disciples

explanation: People with leprosy were excluded from society. Touching him showed compassion and acceptance.

stem: 'Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends' (John 15:13). Christians see this fulfilled in

options.text: the feeding of the five thousand

explanation: Christians believe Jesus' sacrificial death is the greatest act of love.

stem: Complete the verse from 1 John 4:8: 'Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is …'
explanation: 'God is love' (1 John 4:8) is the foundation of Christian teaching on love.

stem: What does the Parable of the Prodigal (Lost) Son teach about love?

options.text: God's love depends on good behaviour
Wealth is a sign of God's love
God, like the father, lovingly forgives those who return and repent

explanation: The father runs to welcome his returning son, which shows God's forgiving love (Luke 15:11–32).

stem: Which is an example of a church showing Christian love in Botswana today?

options.text: Running home-based care for people living with HIV/AIDS

explanation: Caring for the sick and vulnerable puts agape love into practice.

stem: Which value in Setswana culture overlaps most closely with Christian love of neighbour?
explanation: Botho (humanity, respect and kindness towards others) closely matches love of neighbour.

stem: In John 13:34–35, what did Jesus say would show the world that people are his disciples?
explanation: The 'new commandment': love one another as I have loved you; by this everyone will know you are my disciples.

stem: Which of these is a challenge to practising Christian love in modern society?
explanation: Materialism and selfishness put the self first, which goes against self-giving agape love.

stem: Love is at the centre of Christian teaching.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State three Christian teachings about love. Support each with a Bible reference.
parts.markScheme: 1 mark each for a teaching with a correct supporting reference, e.g. love God and neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39); love one another as Jesus loved (John 13:34); love your enemies (Matthew 5:44); God is love (1 John 4:8); God so loved the world (John 3:16); love is patient and kind (1 Corinthians 13:4–7); your neighbour is anyone in need (Luke 10:25–37).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two ways in which Jesus demonstrated love through his life.
parts.markScheme: 2 marks per way: identify the action with an example [1] and explain how it shows love [1], e.g. healing a leper, accepting an outcast [1+1]; washing disciples' feet, humble service [1+1]; forgiving those who crucified him [1+1]; eating with Zacchaeus, accepting sinners [1+1]; dying on the cross, self-sacrifice [1+1]; feeding the 5000, compassion for the hungry [1+1].

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss how far Christian love is practised in Botswana today.
parts.markScheme: Level-based: 3 marks for a balanced discussion with examples on both sides and a conclusion, e.g. church home-based care and charity, botho, forgiveness vs gender-based violence, selfishness and materialism, neglect of the elderly. 2 marks: examples on one side only, or both sides with no conclusion. 1 mark: a simple relevant point.

stem: 'Christian love is the answer to the social problems facing Botswana today.' Discuss.

parts.prompt: Write an essay responding to this statement.
parts.markScheme: Levels of response. Level 5 (21–25): accurate, well-referenced teachings on love (e.g. Matthew 22, 1 Corinthians 13, Luke 10, John 13); clear application to named Botswana problems (e.g. HIV/AIDS, gender-based violence, poverty, corruption, family breakdown); balanced evaluation, including limits (some problems also need government action, laws, economic change; not everyone is Christian); reasoned conclusion. Level 4 (16–20): good knowledge and application, evaluation less developed. Level 3 (11–15): relevant knowledge with some application, mostly descriptive. Level 2 (6–10): limited, general knowledge with little application. Level 1 (1–5): a few relevant points. Teacher to confirm against the BEC level descriptors in section 4 of the syllabus.

stem: A wheelbarrow is an example of which class of lever?
explanation: The load (in the barrow) is between the fulcrum (the wheel) and the effort (the handles), so it is 2nd class.

stem: In a 3rd-class lever, which is in the middle?
explanation: In 3rd-class levers (tweezers, fishing rod), the effort is between the fulcrum and the load.

stem: Which type of motion is a sewing-machine needle moving up and down?
explanation: Backwards-and-forwards motion in a straight line is reciprocating.

stem: Mechanical advantage is calculated as

options.text: distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load

explanation: MA = load ÷ effort. The third option is the formula for velocity ratio.

stem: A lever lifts a 300 N load placed 0.2 m from the fulcrum. The effort is applied 1.2 m from the fulcrum. What effort is needed?
A machine has an MA of 3.2 and a VR of 4. What is its efficiency?
explanation: Efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100 = 3.2 ÷ 4 × 100 = 80%.

stem: A 20-tooth driver gear turning at 300 rpm drives a 60-tooth gear. What is the speed of the driven gear?
explanation: Gear ratio = 60 ÷ 20 = 3:1, so output speed = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm.

stem: Why is an idler gear placed between a driver and a driven gear?

options.text: To convert rotary motion to linear
To reduce the number of teeth
To make both gears turn in the same direction

explanation: An idler reverses the direction of rotation so that the driver and driven turn the same way. It does not change the ratio.

stem: Which gears change the direction of rotation through 90°, as in a hand drill?
explanation: Bevel gears have cone-shaped teeth that transmit rotation between shafts at right angles.

stem: A single-start worm turning at 800 rpm drives a 40-tooth worm wheel. What is the speed of the wheel?
explanation: Ratio = 40:1 for a single-start worm, so 800 ÷ 40 = 20 rpm.

stem: A 50 mm driver pulley turning at 1200 rpm drives a 150 mm pulley. What is the speed of the driven pulley?
explanation: Output = 1200 × 50 ÷ 150 = 400 rpm. The larger driven pulley turns more slowly.

stem: A cam and follower converts
explanation: The rotating cam pushes the follower up and down (reciprocating).

stem: What is one advantage of a chain and sprocket over a belt and pulley?
explanation: A chain gives a positive drive with no slip. It is noisier, more expensive and needs lubrication.

stem: Why is the efficiency of a real machine always less than 100%?

options.text: Energy is wasted overcoming friction, as heat and sound
The effort is always greater than the load

explanation: Friction converts some input energy into heat and sound, so less useful work comes out.

stem: A small motor must open a model gate slowly, and the gate must not move when the power is off. Which mechanism is most suitable?
explanation: A worm and wheel gives a large speed reduction and cannot be driven backwards, so the gate stays locked.

stem: Levers are classified by the positions of the fulcrum, load and effort.

parts.prompt: Name the class of lever for each of: (i) a pair of pliers, (ii) a bottle opener, (iii) a pair of tweezers.
parts.markScheme: (i) 1st class [1]; (ii) 2nd class [1]; (iii) 3rd class [1].

stem: A pulley system lifts a load of 400 N with an effort of 125 N. The effort moves 4 m while the load rises 1 m.

parts.prompt: Calculate (i) the mechanical advantage, (ii) the velocity ratio, (iii) the efficiency.

stem: Bicycles use a chain and sprocket rather than a belt and pulley.

parts.prompt: Give two reasons why.
parts.markScheme: Any two: no slip / positive drive [1]; can transmit larger forces [1]; less affected by wet or muddy conditions [1]; chain can be changed or repaired easily [1].

stem: A small business in Maun wants a motorised display stand that slowly rotates a craft basket so customers can see all sides. The electric motor turns at 1200 rpm. The display turntable must rotate at about 10 rpm, quietly and safely.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the input motion and the output motion needed.
parts.markScheme: Input: rotary (high speed) [1]; output: rotary (slow) [1].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the overall speed reduction ratio needed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A designer suggests a single-start worm on the motor shaft driving a worm wheel, followed by a pair of spur gears. The worm wheel has 40 teeth. What gear ratio must the spur-gear stage give? Suggest suitable tooth numbers for the driver and driven spur gears.
parts.markScheme: Worm stage = 40:1 [1]; remaining ratio = 120 ÷ 40 = 3:1 [1]; suitable pair, e.g. 20-tooth driver and 60-tooth driven (or 15 and 45) [1]; driven larger than driver [1].

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Give two reasons why a worm and wheel is suitable for this product.
parts.markScheme: Two reasons, each explained: large speed reduction in a compact space [2]; quiet, smooth running [2]; cannot be back-driven, so the turntable will not turn by hand and strain the motor [2]; gives a right-angle drive, so the motor can lie flat under the base [2].

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Describe, with notes, how the turntable could be supported so that it turns smoothly and safely. Include one safety feature.
parts.markScheme: Up to 5 for a clear description, e.g. central shaft in a bearing or bush [1]; lazy-Susan ball race or thrust bearing to carry the load [1]; lubrication or low-friction material such as nylon [1]; gears enclosed in a guard or housing [1]; low voltage / insulated wiring / fuse or switch [1]. Award sketches with notes if used.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Suggest one other mechanism that could replace the spur-gear stage, and give one disadvantage of it.
parts.markScheme: Belt and pulley (or chain and sprocket) [1] with correct diameter/teeth ratio idea [1]; disadvantage, e.g. belt can slip, which affects speed; chain is noisy and needs lubrication [1].
